title: Second-Order Effects
intro: The square law is only a first approximation. A handful of corrections explain most of the surprises in real circuits.

blocks.text: When the source voltage rises above the bulk (VSB > 0), the depletion region under the channel grows and more gate voltage is needed to invert the channel, so VTH rises:

blocks.source: VTH = VTH0 + gamma * [ sqrt(2*PhiF + VSB) - sqrt(2*PhiF) ]

blocks.text: gamma (about 0.3 to 0.6 V^(1/2)) is the body-effect coefficient and 2*PhiF is about 0.7 to 0.9 V. The body acts like a second, weaker gate, adding a transconductance gmb = eta * gm with eta = gamma / (2*sqrt(2*PhiF + VSB)), typically 0.1 to 0.3. It matters most for source followers and any device whose source is not at the bulk potential.

As VDS rises above Vov the pinch-off point moves toward the source, shortening the effective channel and raising the current: ID = (1/2)*mu_n*Cox*(W/L)*Vov^2*(1 + lambda*VDS). lambda is roughly inversely proportional to L, so long devices have flatter output curves and higher output resistance ro = 1 / (lambda*ID), at the cost of speed and area.

Below threshold the current does not drop to zero but decays exponentially: ID is proportional to exp(VGS / (zeta*VT)), where VT = kT/q is about 26 mV at room temperature and zeta is about 1.2 to 1.5. This corresponds to roughly 80 to 100 mV of gate voltage per decade of current. In this regime gm = ID / (zeta*VT), the highest gm per unit current the device can offer.

items: Velocity saturation and mobility degradation make ID grow linearly rather than quadratically with Vov: the 'square law' becomes closer to a 'linear law' at high overdrive.
Drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL) makes VTH fall as VDS rises, reducing ro.
Hot-carrier effects and gate leakage set limits on the supply voltage and add noise.

blocks.text: Practical rule: use the square law to get an initial sizing, then rely on simulation with foundry models to finish the design. The first-order equations are for insight, not for final numbers.

blocks.title: Body effect on VTH
blocks.text: VTH0 = 0.4 V, gamma = 0.4 V^(1/2), 2*PhiF = 0.8 V. Find VTH when VSB = 0.8 V.
solution: sqrt(0.8 + 0.8) = 1.265 and sqrt(0.8) = 0.894, a difference of 0.371.
blocks.hint: Plug straight into the VTH expression.

blocks.title: Output resistance
blocks.text: A transistor carries ID = 200 uA with lambda = 0.1 V^-1. Find ro. What happens to ro if L is doubled at the same current (lambda scales as 1/L)?
solution: Doubling L halves lambda to 0.05 V^-1, so ro = 100 kohm.
blocks.answer: ro = 50 kohm; doubling L gives 100 kohm.

blocks.title: Weak inversion gm
blocks.text: In weak inversion with zeta = 1.4 and VT = 26 mV, what is gm for ID = 10 uA? Compare to 2*ID/Vov with Vov = 0.2 V.
solution: Strong inversion at the same current: 2*10 uA / 0.2 V = 0.1 mS. So weak inversion gives about 2.7 times more gm for the same current, but needs a very large W/L.
